explain: Offline writes rule out any model that needs a quorum, so linearizable and sequential are out. With replicas accepting writes independently, concurrent edits will conflict, and convergence requires a deterministic merge (a CRDT or last-writer-wins, which can drop data).

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
question: A counter key receives 50,000 increments per second; a shard can absorb 8,000 writes per second. Which fix actually works?
options: Add more shards to the ring
Give the shard more virtual nodes
Split the counter into 10 sub-counters with suffixes and sum them on read
Put a client-side read cache in front of it
explain: A single key lives on one shard, so more shards or tokens cannot divide its traffic. A read cache does nothing for writes. Splitting into 10 sub-keys spreads about 5,000 writes per second to each (if they hash to different shards), and the price is that a read must fetch and add all 10.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Weighting soft scores with function_score and phased ranking
question: In our function_score query, what is the effect of `"boost_mode": "replace"`?
options: The final score is the combined function score; the wrapped query's score is ignored
The filters are replaced by the functions
Each function's weight replaces its own output
Missing fields are replaced by the origin
explain: boost_mode decides how the function result combines with the query score; replace uses only the function score. Here the wrapped query is filter-only and scores 0, so the default multiply would make every final score 0.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
question: In the example, what makes x5 the first UIP of the conflict?
options: It was the first literal assigned at level 3
It is the only level-3 node that every path from the decision x3 to the conflict passes through, closest to the conflict
It appears in the most clauses of the formula
It has the highest VSIDS activity
explain: A unique implication point at the conflict level is a node every path from that level's decision to the conflict goes through. The decision x3 is always one; the first UIP is the one nearest the conflict, here x5. Cutting there gives (not x4 or not x5), which is shorter and more general than the decision-only clause.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
question: Your scanner reports no vulnerabilities for an image built last month. What should you conclude?
options: The image has no bugs
No currently published advisory matches a package the scanner recognised; rescan regularly because new CVEs are published every day
The image will stay clean
Scanning is unnecessary for this image
explain: A scan is a snapshot against today's databases and only covers packages it can identify. New advisories appear constantly, so running images need continuous rescanning.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
question: Your cluster's kubelets run without seccompDefault. A pod spec sets no seccompProfile. Which seccomp profile does it get?
options: RuntimeDefault
Docker's default profile
Unconfined
Localhost
explain: The Kubernetes seccomp tutorial says pods use RuntimeDefault by default only when seccompDefault is enabled; otherwise the default is Unconfined. Set it in the pod or enable the kubelet option.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
question: A namespace has `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A user applies a Deployment whose pod template sets `privileged: true`. What happens?
options: The Deployment is accepted, but its pods are rejected when the ReplicaSet tries to create them
PSA mutates the template to remove privileged
The pods start but are killed after 60 seconds
The Deployment is rejected immediately
explain: The PSA docs state enforce applies only to the resulting pod objects, while audit and warn also apply to workload resources. PSA validates; it never mutates.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
question: Which control blocked CVE-2019-5736 even on unpatched runc, according to the advisory?
options: Network policies
The default AppArmor profile
A read-only root filesystem
User namespaces where the host's root is not mapped into the container
explain: The advisory says it is not blocked by the default AppArmor policy but is blocked by correct use of user namespaces: container root is then not host root, so it cannot write the host runc binary.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
question: The last instruction in a build deletes a 300 MB cache directory that an earlier instruction created. What happens to the size of the pushed image?
options: It shrinks by 300 MB, because the final filesystem no longer contains the directory
The build fails, because whiteouts may not refer to lower layers
The earlier layer is rewritten without the directory
A new layer of whiteouts is added; the 300 MB stays in the earlier blob and is still pulled
explain: A removal is recorded as a whiteout in the new layer, and whiteouts only hide names in lower layers. The earlier blob is immutable and content addressed, so it still holds the bytes and is still downloaded. To avoid shipping them, create and delete within one layer, or build in one stage and copy only the output into a second.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Autoscaling and GPU scheduling: two control loops
question: A Deployment runs 4 replicas, each container requesting 500m CPU. The HPA targets 50% average utilization and the pods average 400m. What does the controller write, and does it keep scaling?
options: 6 now, then 7 on the next tick
8, doubling because utilization is 80%
7, and it stops: at 7 replicas the ratio is 0.914, inside the default 0.1 tolerance
5, because the controller adds at most one replica per period
explain: The target per pod is 50% of the 500m request, so 250m. The ratio is 400 / 250 = 1.6 and the ceiling of 4 x 1.6 = 6.4 is 7. If total demand is unchanged, 7 pods average 1600 / 7 = 228.57m, a ratio of 0.914, which is 0.086 from 1.0 and inside the tolerance, so the loop settles. A later scale down would additionally wait out the 300 s stabilization window.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
question: Which use of *those* should become a filter edit rather than a frozen set of ids?
options: save those
email me those
only those that are remote
compare those
explain: *only those that are remote* narrows the search, and should keep working as postings change, so it is a constraint added to the filters. Saving, emailing and comparing act on the specific items on screen.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
question: A team paraphrases its reasoning model's scratchpad paragraph by paragraph at inference time, and MATH accuracy drops 7%. What should they conclude?
options: Not much yet: unfamiliar-looking scratchpads can distract the model, so compare training on paraphrased versus original scratchpads before inferring encoding
The model uses encoded reasoning, since meaning was preserved and accuracy fell
The model uses filler-token computation
The paraphraser is too weak and must be replaced with a stronger model
explain: Anthropic found that merely splitting the scratchpad into blocks, with no paraphrasing, cut MATH pass@1 by 7%. A drop at inference time has innocent causes. Distilling paraphrased scratchpads into a model and comparing accuracy controls for that. A stronger paraphraser cannot be trusted not to share the code.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
question: Which misbehavior is a CoT monitor most likely to catch in a current reasoning model?
options: Choosing an answer because a metadata tag in the prompt says so
Agreeing with a user's stated opinion on a multiple-choice question
Reporting a slightly wrong number in a results table
Finding and exploiting a multi-step bug in a test harness that requires exploring several files
explain: The test-harness exploit needs exploration and planning, which must pass through the CoT, and Baker et al. caught such hacks at high rates. The other three can be done in a single forward pass (Chen et al.'s hints, Turpin's sycophancy) or need little reasoning (Emmons et al.'s example of faking a table entry), so silence is the default.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
question: You create four streams with cudaStreamCreate and issue, per chunk: H2D, kernel, D2H. Between chunk 1 and chunk 2 you add a cudaMemcpy (no stream) for a small constant buffer. What happens?
options: That copy is on the NULL stream, so it waits for all four blocking streams to drain and everything after it waits for the copy
Nothing changes; a small copy cannot affect scheduling
Only chunk 2's H2D is delayed, by the length of the small copy
The four streams keep overlapping but the results of chunk 1 become undefined
explain: The legacy default stream is a blocking stream: it waits for all other blocking streams, and they wait for it. Two operations from different streams cannot run concurrently if any NULL stream operation is submitted in between. The small copy becomes a full barrier. Creating the streams with cudaStreamNonBlocking, or compiling with --default-stream per-thread, removes it.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: In an inference server: double buffering and reading the gaps
question: Why does double buffering need two pinned buffers rather than one, if the copy is asynchronous anyway?
options: Because the host would otherwise overwrite bytes the copy engine is still reading, so it must wait for the copy to finish before preparing the next chunk
A single pinned buffer cannot be larger than one page-locked allocation
Because each CUDA stream requires its own pinned allocation
Because cudaMemcpyAsync needs a separate destination buffer per call
explain: Asynchrony means the host returns early, not that the buffer is free. With one buffer the host must wait until the engine has finished reading it, which rebuilds the serial schedule. A second buffer lets the host fill B while the engine drains A; an event records when A is released.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: From [CLS] to a score: logits, sigmoid and monoT5's true token
question: In monoT5, why does ranking by the softmax over all vocabulary tokens work poorly compared with the two-token softmax?
options: Because the vocabulary softmax is too slow to compute
Because probability mass on thousands of unrelated tokens varies across inputs and swamps the true versus false comparison
Because T5 cannot output the word true
Because the vocabulary softmax is not differentiable
explain: The paper reports near-zero metrics for that variant. Restricting to the two target tokens turns the output into a clean binary decision, sigma(z_true minus z_false), that is comparable across candidates.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes, hex and XOR: the alphabet of cryptography
question: What is 0x0F XOR 0xFF?
options: 0xFF
0xF0
0x0F
explain: 0x0F is 00001111 and 0xFF is 11111111. Every bit of 0x0F is flipped by the all-ones key, giving 11110000, which is 0xF0.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Modes of operation: why ECB leaks and what CBC and CTR fix
question: Which property of ECB made the Adobe password file useful to attackers without decrypting anything?
options: 3DES has a short block size
Identical passwords produced identical ciphertexts, so users could be grouped and their hints pooled
The IV was published
The ciphertext was longer than the password
explain: ECB is deterministic per block. Grouping equal ciphertexts and reading all the hints for a group gave away common passwords, no key needed.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
question: Why does HMAC resist length extension while SHA-256(key + message) does not?
options: HMAC uses a longer key
HMAC's output comes from a second, keyed hash, so the published value is not a state anyone can continue
HMAC encrypts the message
HMAC uses MD5 internally
explain: In the naive design the tag is the final state of a hash over attacker-extendable input. HMAC's outer keyed hash means the tag is not a resumable state of the inner computation.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
question: Why must RSA encryption be randomised (OAEP) rather than computed as m^e mod n?
options: Because m^e is too slow
Without randomness, equal messages give equal ciphertexts, so an attacker can confirm guesses by encrypting them with the public key
Because e is too small
Because n must change every message
explain: The public key is public, so anyone can encrypt candidate plaintexts and compare. Randomised padding makes each encryption different.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Unauthenticated encryption: why decryption must refuse first
question: A service encrypts records with AES-CTR and no MAC, and decrypts whatever the client sends back. What does the attacker gain by modifying a ciphertext?
options: The server processes plaintext the attacker shaped, and its reactions can be observed
Nothing, because without the key the result is random noise
The attacker immediately learns the AES key
Only the ability to crash the server
explain: Unauthenticated decryption never refuses, so the server acts on modified plaintext. In CTR a bit flip in the ciphertext flips the same plaintext bit, and the server's reaction (accept, reject, which error) leaks information. The key itself is not revealed; that is not needed for damage.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Fixed IVs in homemade protocols: Zerologon
question: Netlogon also mixed fresh random challenges into the session key. Why did that not save the fixed-IV design?
options: Because the challenges were only 4 bytes long
Because the weakness held for about 1 in 256 keys, the client chose its own input, and unlimited retries let an attacker keep trying fresh keys
Because AES-CFB8 is broken regardless of IV
Because the session key was sent in plaintext
explain: Fresh challenges give a fresh session key per attempt, but with a constant IV and an attacker-chosen plaintext, about one key in 256 produces the predictable output. Without a limit on attempts, a few hundred tries suffice. AES-CFB8 with unique random IVs is not known to be broken.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: MAC constructions: length extension, ambiguity and replay
question: A payment webhook signs `HMAC(key, amount + currency + account)` with plain string concatenation. Which problem remains even though HMAC is correct?
options: Length extension
Field boundaries are ambiguous, so different field values can produce the same signed string
HMAC-SHA-256 is too short
The tag reveals the key
explain: HMAC resists length extension, but without separators or length prefixes `amount=10, currency=0USD` and `amount=100, currency=USD` glue into the same bytes. Sign a canonical encoding with explicit boundaries.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
question: For M = N = 4096, K = 4096 and a 128x128x64 CTA tile, how many mainloop iterations does each CTA execute?
explain: The mainloop walks K in steps of bK: 4096 / 64 = 64 k-tiles. 1024 is the number of CTAs (32 x 32 output tiles), not iterations per CTA.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
question: In PipelineTmaAsync, why can producer_commit be a no-op?
options: Because consumers never wait on the full barrier
Because TMA copies are synchronous
Because the TMA unit itself signals the stage's full barrier when the bytes arrive
Because the producer and consumer are the same warp
explain: The CUTLASS pipeline docs note that commit may be a no-op when producer instructions update the barrier automatically, as TMA does by completing a transaction on the stage's barrier. The consumer still waits on that full barrier.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
question: Pond's 16-socket pool adds 25 ns more than the 8-socket pool. Where does that time come from in the model?
options: Slower DRAM chips in the pool
A CXL switch with arbitration
A retimer to keep the signal clean over a longer distance
Software page-table walks on the remote host
explain: The DRAM and controller budget is identical (45 ns). The 16-socket layout needs longer links, so a retimer (5 + 20 + 5 ns) replaces the 5 ns flight time: 30 - 5 = 25 ns more. A switch is only needed for the larger 32 to 64 socket pools.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The CFAA: access, authorisation, damage and loss
question: Which cost is clearly 'loss' under 18 U.S.C. 1030(e)(11)?
options: The price of the attacker's laptop
The time staff spent responding to the intrusion and restoring the system
The company's future marketing budget
Nothing, unless data was deleted
explain: The definition lists responding to an offence, conducting a damage assessment, restoring data and systems, and revenue lost or costs incurred because of an interruption of service. It does not require deleted data.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
question: What does an Article 29 preservation request achieve on its own?
options: It hands the data to the requesting country immediately
It extradites the suspect
It stops the data being deleted while the formal mutual legal assistance request is prepared
It makes the conduct a crime in both countries
explain: Preservation freezes the data; disclosure needs a separate, formal request processed under the requested country's law. The Senate summary describes at least sixty days to submit that request after preservation.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
question: Why does the pseudonymisation code use HMAC with a secret key rather than plain SHA-256 of the IP address?
options: HMAC is faster
Plain SHA-256 cannot be computed for IP addresses
With so few possible IPv4 addresses, an unkeyed hash can be reversed by hashing them all; the key prevents that
HMAC encrypts the address so it can be decrypted later
explain: The input space is small (about 4.3 billion IPv4 addresses), so a dictionary of all hashes is easy. A keyed HMAC is still one-way and still stable, but only the key holder can produce or check pseudonyms.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
question: A company is under attack from a server in another country. An engineer proposes logging into that server with a leaked password to delete the stolen data. What does the course say?
options: It is lawful self-defence
It is lawful if the data is the company's own
It is lawful if done quickly
It is unauthorised access in probably several jurisdictions, and the server may belong to another victim; preserve evidence and go to law enforcement or the host
explain: CyBOK describes hack-back as squarely within crimes against information systems, open to prosecution in several countries. Recovering your own data does not authorise access to someone else's computer.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
question: Which step of DoReMi needs the Group DRO optimizer?
options: Only step 3, the large main model
Steps 1 and 3
All three steps
Only step 2, the small proxy model
explain: Step 1 is ordinary training of the reference model, and step 3 is ordinary training of the main model on resampled data. Only the small proxy in step 2 uses the min-max objective, which is why the expensive run needs no special code.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: You must choose between two filtered web corpora for a 1B model and can afford only small runs. What does DataDecide suggest?
options: Train ten 10M models and extrapolate a scaling law to 1B
Compare raw accuracy of 20M models on MMLU
Pick the larger corpus, since size predicts quality
Train one 150M model per corpus and compare continuous likelihood metrics such as the probability of correct answers
explain: A single small scale picked the 1B winner about 80 percent of the time, and no scaling-law method beat it for the same compute. Continuous likelihood metrics are far more predictable than accuracy, which is near chance for tiny models on hard benchmarks.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
question: A loop over 1,000,000 AoS particles (32 bytes each) reads only `mass`. You move `mass` into its own float array. Roughly how many cache lines does the pass read now, assuming 64-byte lines?
options: 62,500, because each line now holds 16 masses instead of 2
500,000, because the number of particles did not change
250,000, because each line now holds twice as many masses
1,000,000, because each mass is a separate access
explain: The mass array is 4 MB. 4,000,000 bytes / 64 bytes per line = 62,500 lines. In AoS each line carried 2 masses, so the pass cost 500,000 lines. Lines are the unit of traffic, not elements.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
question: In a Unity chunk, your code saved "entity e5 is at index 5" before e1 was destroyed. What is true afterwards?
options: Index 5 still holds e5
Index 5 now holds e1
e5 has moved to index 1, because the last entity fills the gap
The chunk keeps a hole at index 1 until it is compacted later
explain: Unity keeps chunk arrays tightly packed by moving the last entity into the freed slot. Indices inside a chunk are therefore not stable identities; use entity IDs for that.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
question: An app keeps ID photos 'until verification is complete', but the deletion job only runs on the main bucket. Which copy most extends the exposure window?
options: The main bucket
The user's phone
The TLS session used for upload
The backup set with its own longer retention, plus any copies in tickets or exports
explain: Exposure lasts as long as the longest-lived copy. Backups and side-effect copies have their own retention, and nobody deletes them when the main record goes. The upload session is gone in seconds; the phone is outside the company's control and is not a copy the company holds.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap
question: How should a DBA let a role read every column of `customers` except `ssn` in PostgreSQL?
options: GRANT SELECT on the table, then REVOKE SELECT (ssn)
GRANT SELECT on the table and tell users not to query ssn
Rename the ssn column
GRANT SELECT (id, name, email, created_at) on the table, listing only the allowed columns
explain: A table-level grant covers every column, and a column-level revoke does not subtract from it, as PostgreSQL's documentation warns and the demo shows. List the allowed columns, or publish a view.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme
question: Why does an insider risk tool want an HR connector for departing users?
options: Because a resignation or termination date is the triggering context that makes download spikes and USB copies meaningful
To read employees' performance reviews in full
To revoke access automatically on the first day of employment
Because HR systems contain the DLP policies
explain: Departure is the context in which unusual data activity is most significant; Purview's 'Data theft by departing users' template takes that trigger from an HR connector (or from Entra account deletion). It does not need full reviews, and access removal is a separate identity process.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: An alarm nobody should trip: why deception detects
question: Which item is a honeytoken rather than a honeypot?
options: A virtual machine running a fake SSH service
A whole subnet of decoy servers
A fake AWS access key left in a deployment script
A real server with extra logging
explain: A honeytoken is decoy data (a credential, file, record or URL). A fake service or a network of decoy machines is a honeypot or honeynet; a real server with logging is just monitoring.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: DNS canaries: tripwires that escape locked-down networks
question: Why might a second lookup of the same token, ten seconds after the first, produce no alert?
options: The resolver answered from its cache, so the question never reached your name server
DNS canaries only work once
The token expired
DNS is unreliable and drops half of all queries
explain: Resolvers cache answers for the record's TTL. Low TTLs help, but the first lookup is the reliable signal.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Alert fidelity: false triggers, fingerprinting and upkeep
question: A canary link in a bait email fires two seconds after delivery from your mail provider's address range. What should you do?
options: Delete the token; it is broken
Add the provider's range to a filter that drops all alerts from it
Label the alert as a probable link-scanner fetch, keep it, and treat any later fetch from elsewhere as high priority
Declare an incident: someone read the email in two seconds
explain: Link scanners detonate URLs on delivery, so the first hit is expected. Dropping that range would also hide an attacker who uses the same service later; labelling keeps the signal.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Where a GPU inference stack loses bitwise equality
question: A team sets torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True and finds that two runs of the same model on the same machine give different outputs. What is happening?
options: cuDNN silently drops to a lower precision while benchmarking.
Benchmarking reseeds the RNG, so the weights initialize differently.
Timing noise can make the benchmark pick a different algorithm on a later run, and different algorithms accumulate in different orders.
The GPU clock frequency changes the hardware rounding mode.
explain: The benchmark times candidate algorithms and keeps the winner per shape. Noise in that timing can crown a different winner on another run, and two algorithms with different reduction trees give different bits. Setting benchmark = False pins the choice, but the pinned algorithm may itself be nondeterministic unless the deterministic flags are set too.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
question: Jepsen-style fault injection and DST both inject partitions and crashes into real code. What does DST add that changes day-to-day debugging most?
options: It tests a formal model instead of the code, so it is exhaustive
Any failing run can be replayed exactly from its seed
It needs no changes to how the system does I/O
It runs on real hardware, so timing is realistic
explain: Determinism is the key addition: a failure becomes a seed you can replay, step through and add logging to. DST does test the real code (not a model), it usually *does* require routing I/O through simulated interfaces, and its timing is simulated, not real.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
question: Which system is the *weakest* fit for designing DST in from the start?
options: A new replicated log written in-house with its own network and disk layer
A large existing service built on many third-party clients, thread pools and direct system calls
A consensus library whose I/O already goes through small traits
A storage engine with a single-threaded event loop
explain: Designing DST in requires every source of nondeterminism to be pluggable, which is hard to retrofit across many dependencies and threads. The Antithesis docs call it generally impractical for systems already in production; that is the case a deterministic hypervisor targets. The other three are close to the FoundationDB and TigerBeetle shape.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
question: A deploy key is stored as a JSON document with three fields in one secret. A tool prints the parsed `private_key` field on error. What happens in the log?
options: It is probably shown: redaction matches the exact stored string, and one field of the parsed JSON is a different string
It is masked, because the whole secret is masked
The job fails before printing
GitHub deletes the log automatically
explain: GitHub warns that structured data makes redaction fail because redaction largely relies on finding an exact match. Store each sensitive value as its own secret.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
question: A reviewer reads only the HCL diff in a PR, which changes a variable default from `10.0.0.0/16` to a module input. Why should the pipeline also check the plan JSON?
options: The plan JSON holds the resolved values, such as the CIDR the module actually produces, while the HCL only shows a reference
The HCL diff is always longer
Plan JSON is required by Git
HCL cannot contain security groups
explain: Values from variables, modules and data sources are only known after planning. Scanning the plan catches what the source hides behind references.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Sentinel, enforcement levels and guardrails developers accept
question: A new rule would block 40 pull requests a week across the company, and nobody has seen its results yet. Which enforcement level should it start at?
options: Hard mandatory, so the problem is fixed fastest
Advisory, to measure impact and fix false positives before anything blocks
Soft mandatory with no override permission
No policy at all
explain: Advisory is Sentinel's default and lets a policy fail with a warning. Starting there turns the unknown 40 a week into a measured list before teams are blocked.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
question: What does the 'absorbing state' in masked diffusion refer to?
options: The final layer of the Transformer that absorbs all positional information
The [MASK] token: once the forward process masks a token, it stays masked
The end-of-sequence token that stops generation
A Gaussian noise vector added to token embeddings
explain: In D3PM's absorbing-state process every token moves to [MASK] at some point and never leaves it. At the final time the sequence is entirely masked, which gives a simple known starting point for generation.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
question: You set Fast-dLLM's threshold so that, in a hard reasoning span, no masked token reaches it. What does the sampler do?
options: It commits the single most confident token, so it degrades gracefully to one token per pass
It stalls until the model becomes more confident
It commits every token in the block anyway
It restarts the block with a new random seed
explain: The threshold rule always unmasks the highest-confidence token to guarantee progress. In uncertain regions the sampler becomes sequential, which is exactly where dependencies between tokens matter most.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: Your summarization service has a 15 s TTFT SLO and a 0.15 s TPOT SLO. Attainment is failing. Which change most likely helps?
options: Protect decode steps from long prefills (separate decode GPUs or smaller prefill chunks)
Give prefill more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT
Lower the TTFT SLO to 5 s
Batch more prompts into each prefill
explain: With a 15 s TTFT budget, prefill is rarely the binding constraint. The long documents create long prefills that stall decode steps and break the TPOT SLO, which DistServe observed for vLLM on LongBench, a benchmark of long-document tasks. Shielding decode is the fix; batching more prompts would make the stalls worse.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
question: After a product launch, prompts get 4x longer while output lengths stay the same. In a disaggregated deployment with a load-based autoscaler, which pool should grow, and which signal moves first?
options: Decode, first seen as rising TPOT
Neither: the P:D ratio depends only on the request rate
Prefill, first seen as queued prefill tokens and rising TTFT; decode KV utilization climbs later as the larger caches arrive
Both equally, first seen as GPU utilization
explain: Prefill work per request grows at least 4x (more with attention), so the prefill share of GPU time rises, as in the 08 to 14 window of the timeline. Requests queue at prefill before anything reaches decode, so queued prefill tokens and TTFT move first, the signal Dynamo's load-based planner watches. Each request also brings 4x more KV, so decode KV-cache utilization rises next and decode may need capacity too.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through
question: After deletion, which piece of the PHOTO.JPG directory entry is gone for good?
options: The first character of its name
Its size
Its first cluster number
Its extension
explain: Deletion overwrote only the name's first byte with 0xE5. Size, first cluster and extension remain, which is why tools show deleted names as ?HOTO.JPG or _HOTO.JPG.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal
question: With the default data=ordered journal mode, what can the ext4 journal give you after a file is deleted?
options: Possibly an older copy of the metadata block holding the file's inode, with its extents
A full copy of the file's content
Nothing, because the journal is erased on deletion
The user name of whoever deleted it
explain: data=ordered sends metadata, not file data, through the journal. Older inode blocks in the journal can point recovery tools to the content blocks. ext4 does not log who deleted a file.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
question: The USB stick is lost. What can still show that the user browsed its folder `E:\Q3`?
options: Only the stick itself
The master file table of the laptop's C: drive
SRUM
ShellBags in the user's hives, and LNK and Jump List entries pointing to `E:\Q3`
explain: ShellBags record navigated folders, and LNK and Jump List entries record opened files with their paths and volume serial, all stored on the laptop. The laptop's C: MFT does not index files on E:.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
question: Why does wiping a file often fail to hide that something was wiped?
options: Wiping tools are blocked by NTFS
The wipe overwrites the content but leaves traces such as the tool's execution artefacts and change journal records of the overwrite
Wiped data can always be recovered by carving
Windows keeps a copy of every wiped file in SRUM
explain: SP 800-86 notes wiping is effective at preventing collection of the content itself, so carving does not undo it. But running a tool and rewriting a file leave execution and journal traces. SRUM stores usage statistics, not files.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: A DiskANN service is limited by SSD IOPS at peak traffic, and p99 latency is comfortably under target. Which change is most sensible?
options: Increase W from 4 to 16
Increase L to raise recall
Lower W toward 1 to cut total reads per query
Turn off re-ranking
explain: Smaller beams waste fewer reads, so each query consumes less of the IOPS budget; latency rises but there is headroom. The repository docs recommend W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating. Re-ranking costs no extra reads, so disabling it saves nothing.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: In the toy example, what happens to the optimal policy as $\beta$ grows very large?
options: It approaches the reference distribution: 50%, 30%, 20%
It puts all mass on B, the highest reward
It becomes uniform over A, B and C
It puts all mass on A, the reference's favorite
explain: Reweighting by $\exp(r/\beta)$ approaches multiplying everything by 1 as $\beta$ grows, so the optimum returns to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. At $\beta = 10$ it is already 49.38%, 32.75%, 17.87%. Small $\beta$ is what collapses it onto B.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Your feedback log has 2,000 thumbs-up and 20,000 thumbs-down responses. Following the KTO paper's guidance with $\lambda_U = 1$, which $\lambda_D$ is in range?
options: 0.1, to down-weight the rare class
1, the default
explain: The ratio $\lambda_D n_D / (\lambda_U n_U)$ should land in [1, 1.5]. With $n_D/n_U = 0.1$, $\lambda_D$ must be between 10 and 15, so 12 fits. Leaving it at 1 lets the undesirable class dominate the gradient.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Dual writes have been on for a week, but the backfill has not run. A read from the new Subscriptions table for a customer who subscribed two years ago and has not changed since returns nothing. What happened?
options: The dual write to the new table failed for this customer
Nothing went wrong: untouched old objects only reach the new store through the backfill
The new table needs a read replica before it can serve reads
Dual writes copy old rows lazily on the first read, so the next read will succeed
explain: Dual writes only cover writes made after they were turned on. Stripe also copied objects lazily whenever they were *updated*, but an object nobody touches is copied only by the backfill. This is why reads must not move until the backfill and a completeness check are done.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: Midway through phase 3, the new write path for prorations is found to compute the wrong amount. Most other paths already write the new store first and archive to the old one. What is the safest response?
options: Restore the new store from last night's backup
Pause all writes until the bug is fixed
Delete the old store so the two cannot disagree
Flip the prorations path back to the old write order; the old store is still current because every path still writes it
explain: In phase 3 every write still reaches the old store (as the primary or as an archive), so it is complete. Rolling one path back by a flag is cheap. That safety disappears in phase 4, which is why it comes last.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: A read takes exactly 1,024 ns. In which hist() bucket does it appear?
explain: 1024 = 2^10, so b = 10 and the bucket is [2^10, 2^11) = [1K, 2K). Bucket intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound; only 0 and 1 get single-value buckets.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: An activation tensor after ReLU has range [0, 6]. Using asymmetric int8 with q_min = -128, what are S and Z?
explain: S = (6 - 0) / (127 - (-128)) = 6/255 = 0.0235, and Z = round(-128 - 0/S) = -128. Real 0 maps to the lowest code, so all 256 levels cover [0, 6]. The symmetric choice (S = 6/127, Z = 0) would waste the 128 negative codes on values ReLU never produces.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: A wake-word model meets its accuracy target in float but loses 6 points after full-integer PTQ with per-channel weights. Calibration data is representative. What should you try next?
options: Quantization-aware training, or 16-bit activations if the runtime supports them
Per-tensor weights instead of per-channel
Remove calibration and use dynamic range quantization on a microcontroller with no float unit
Prune the model to 90% sparsity
explain: Per-channel weights and good calibration are already in place, so the remaining error likely comes from activations or from a small model's sensitivity. QAT lets the model adapt to rounding, and 16x8 mode reduces activation error. Per-tensor would be worse, and dynamic range keeps float outputs that an integer-only MCU cannot run.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
question: You installed the NetScaler fix on 11 October 2023, the day after it shipped. Why could an attacker still be using your gateway on 20 October?
options: The fix did not install
A session cookie stolen before the fix stayed valid until sessions were killed
The fix turned off MFA
NetScaler cannot be patched
explain: Exploitation began in late August. The fix stops new leaks but does not invalidate tokens already taken; NetScaler's guidance was to kill all active and persistent sessions after updating.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
question: M-Trends 2026 estimates a mean time to exploit of -7 days. What does the negative sign mean for an edge patch process?
options: Patches arrive a week before bugs are found
On average, exploitation begins before a fix exists, so fast patching must be paired with checking for compromise that happened earlier
Attackers stopped using n-days
Vendors publish advisories a week late on purpose
explain: Negative TTE means exploitation precedes the patch. Speed still matters (it stops mass exploitation after disclosure), but forensic triage is what deals with the earlier window.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
question: Barracuda asked customers to replace ESG appliances 'regardless of patch version level'. What does that tell a defender about patching?
options: Patches from Barracuda were never released
Once an appliance may hold persistence the vendor cannot reliably remove, patching cannot restore trust; only new hardware can
Email gateways cannot be patched
Replacement is always cheaper than patching
explain: The patch fixed the bug, but the vendor could not be confident that software updates removed the intruder from compromised devices. The same logic drives rebuilds for Ivanti and hard resets for Cisco.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: A team trains with a hard rule 'reward = -1 if truncated at 8K tokens' and sees training become unstable as responses approach 8K. Which change follows the DAPO findings?
options: Raise the penalty to -10 so the model learns faster
Remove the correctness reward for long responses
Mask truncated samples from the loss, or ramp the penalty linearly over a soft zone before the limit
Lower the learning rate only for long responses
explain: Overlong filtering (masking) and soft overlong punishment both reduce reward noise from punishing reasoning that was merely cut off. A bigger cliff adds more noise, not less.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
question: A gateway blocks paths containing `..`; the app behind it percent-decodes the path and opens the file. Which change actually closes the hole?
options: Make the gateway also block the string `%2e%2e`
Lower-case the path in the gateway before checking
In the app, decode, resolve the full path and check it is inside the base folder before opening
Return a generic error page so attackers learn less
explain: Blocking one encoded spelling leaves the others (`%2E%2e`, double encoding, and more). Resolving and checking the final path in the component that opens the file covers every spelling, because the decision is made on what the path finally means.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
question: Which pair is canonically equivalent (so equal after NFC), not just compatibility equivalent?
options: `ﬁ` (U+FB01) and `fi`
`／` (U+FF0F) and `/`
Ω OHM SIGN (U+2126) and Ω GREEK CAPITAL LETTER OMEGA (U+03A9)
explain: UAX #15 lists the ohm sign as a canonical singleton: it never survives normalisation, even NFC. The ligature, fullwidth solidus and superscript five are compatibility equivalents and change only under NFKC or NFKD.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Confusables and homoglyphs: UTS #39 skeletons
question: `ѕсоре` is written entirely in Cyrillic and `scope` entirely in Latin. Which check flags the pair?
options: A mixed-script check on each string
Comparing their NFKC forms
Comparing their UTS #39 skeletons
Comparing them after `casefold()`
explain: Each string is single-script, so a mixed-script rule passes both. NFKC and case folding leave Cyrillic letters Cyrillic. Only the skeleton, which maps Cyrillic ѕ, с, о, р, е to Latin prototypes, shows they look the same.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: JSON differentials: duplicate keys, numbers and CouchDB
question: Two services read the same JSON body. Service A keeps the first value of a duplicate key, service B the last. Which design removes the disagreement?
options: Reject documents with duplicate keys at the entry point, then forward the parsed object or a canonical re-serialisation
Tell clients not to send duplicates
Make both services keep the first value, by convention
Sort the keys alphabetically
explain: Asking clients to behave does nothing against an attacker. Aligning two parsers by convention breaks again when a library changes. Rejecting at the edge and forwarding only unambiguous data means there is nothing to disagree about.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
question: You find that your login redirect check and the browser disagree on hosts for URLs containing backslashes. After fixing the code, what is the most important next step?
options: Search logs for past redirect parameters whose parsed hosts differed, and review the sessions involved
Close the ticket
Rotate the TLS certificate
Disable all redirects permanently
explain: A differential may have been used before you found it. Replaying stored raw inputs through both parsers tells you whether anyone was sent off-site, which decides the rest of the response.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: A NetworkConnect filter is `onmatch="include"` with two rules: Image ends with `powershell.exe`, and DestinationPort is `443`. Which connection is logged?
options: Only connections made by powershell.exe to port 443
Any connection made by powershell.exe
Any connection to port 443
Every connection, because include with two rules logs all
explain: The two rules are on different fields (Image and DestinationPort), and Sysmon combines different fields with AND. Two rules on the same field would have been ORed.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: Your draft AppLocker policy has run in audit mode for two weeks. Which events tell you what the policy would have broken?
explain: 8003 (EXE or DLL) and 8006 (script or MSI) mean 'allowed, but would have been prevented if enforced', and appear only in audit mode. 8004 and 8007 are actual blocks in enforce mode; 8002 and 8005 are allows.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: An attacker uses only built-in tools (net for accounts and shares, wmic, and ntdsutil, the Active Directory database tool) with valid admin credentials. Why is this hard for an EDR?
options: The telemetry is recorded, but each action resembles normal administration, so detection depends on context and baselines rather than a 'malware' verdict
EDR cannot record built-in tools
Built-in tools disable EDR automatically
Windows hides admin activity from all sensors
explain: The sensor still records the processes and command lines. The difficulty is deciding they are malicious: CISA's living-off-the-land guidance notes that many organisations lack the capabilities to tell such activity from normal administration, which is why baselines of admin behaviour matter.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
question: At minute 47 the meter reads 122 W. Which statement is correct using only that one reading?
options: It must be the fridge, because the fridge draws 120 W
It could be the fridge alone, or two 60 W lamps if the house had two, so one reading cannot decide
It must be the lamp plus 62 W of noise
It is the kettle in a low-power state
explain: A single reading only constrains the sum. With three known appliances, 120 W happens to match one combination, but adding a second 60 W lamp would create a second exact match. Context over time (what changed, and when) is what breaks such ties.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
question: A model reaches F1 0.95 on houses it was trained on and 0.60 on a new house. What is the most useful next step suggested by this course's sources?
options: Report 0.95, since the training houses are representative
Shrink the window to one sample to avoid overfitting
Switch to CO, which needs no training data
Add synthetic aggregates built from activations of many houses and evaluate on a held-out house
explain: Kelly and Knottenbelt found that mixing synthetic aggregates with real data regularised the nets and helped on unseen houses, and both they and Zhang and colleagues test on a held-out house. A one-sample window throws away the context that makes neural NILM work, and CO still needs appliance models learned from sub-metered data.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
question: Why is a missing domain scored as weight 0 rather than with the disagree weight -2.74?
options: Missing data carries no evidence either way; scoring it as disagreement would push true duplicates like r1-r3 toward non-match
Because log2 of zero is undefined
Because Fellegi-Sunter only allows agreement levels
explain: A missing value is neither agreement nor disagreement. Treating it as disagreement subtracts 2.74 and would drop r1-r3 from 0.863 to about 0.49, punishing incomplete records rather than conflicting ones.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: A SaaS vendor's own tenant is breached, and the attacker adds a new client secret to the vendor's multitenant application object. Your tenant granted that app's service principal Mail.Read (application). What is your exposure?
options: None: the secret was added in another tenant
Only mailboxes of users who signed in to the app
The attacker can get app-only tokens for your tenant and read every mailbox the permission covers, until you disable the service principal or remove the grant
None, because application permissions need MFA
explain: The app authenticates with credentials on its application object, wherever that lives, and is authorized by your service principal's grants. Your controls are on your side: the grant, and disabling the service principal.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: An email asks a user to enter a 'Teams meeting ID' at microsoft.com/devicelogin. The user does so and signs in with a FIDO2 key. What happened?
options: Nothing: FIDO2 binds the sign-in to the correct origin, so the attacker gets no tokens
Only an ID token was issued, which cannot read mail
The attacker, who started the device code flow, received tokens for the user; FIDO2 protected the login page but not the flow
The sign-in failed because FIDO2 is not supported for device code flow
explain: The user signed in on the real Microsoft origin, so the passkey worked. The device authorization grant then issued tokens to the client that requested the code: the attacker. Blocking the flow is the control.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: An attacker has Domain Admin on premises. The tenant uses PHS and Seamless SSO, and all Global Administrators are synced accounts. Which change removes the most direct path to Global Administrator?
options: Switching from PHS to PTA
Disabling Teams
Making Global Administrators cloud-only accounts with phishing-resistant MFA, so no on-premises object holds cloud admin rights
Enabling the AD recycle bin
explain: With synced admins, control of AD or the sync server can change those accounts (passwords, soft or hard matching). Microsoft's rule is that no on-premises account should hold Microsoft 365 admin rights. Switching to PTA moves the bridge to new Tier 0 agents; it does not remove it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: A server handles 20,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with one thread per connection. Which cost grows directly with the number of *idle* connections?
options: CPU time spent parsing requests
A sleeping thread, with its own stack and kernel task, for every connection
Network bandwidth used by the replies
The number of bytes each request contains
explain: Parsing and bandwidth scale with *active* traffic. An idle connection does no work, but in thread-per-connection it still owns a whole thread: a stack, a kernel task, and a place in the scheduler. An event loop keeps only a small per-connection record instead.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: A Node service handles 4 slow password hashes (crypto.pbkdf2, about 100 ms each) at the same moment that 4 requests call fs.readFile. With the default pool, what do the file reads experience?
options: They queue behind the hashes on the 4-thread pool, so they finish roughly 100 ms later than they otherwise would
Nothing, file reads use epoll and never touch the pool
They run on the loop thread and block it
Node starts 4 extra threads automatically for file I/O
explain: Both async pbkdf2 and fs calls run on libuv's shared thread pool, which has 4 threads by default. The hashes occupy all 4, so the file reads wait about one hash duration. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or moving hashing elsewhere fixes it. Disk files cannot use epoll at all.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
question: Two systems' per-query nDCG@10 values correlate at 0.9 across 100 queries. Compared with an unpaired bootstrap, what does a paired bootstrap of the mean difference give?
options: A wider interval, because pairing loses degrees of freedom
The same interval, because the means are identical either way
A much narrower interval, because shared query difficulty cancels in the per-query differences
An interval centered on a different value
explain: The point estimate is the same mean difference either way. With strong correlation, most per-query variation is query difficulty that hits both systems alike. Differencing per query removes it, so the variance of the difference is much smaller than the sum of the two variances.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A JIT engine maps one page as readable, writable and executable and keeps writing new code into it while it runs. Which policy does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: W^X, because any memory-write bug could place attacker code in a page that is also executable
ASLR, because the page has a fixed address
RELRO, because the page is writable
None: JIT pages are exempt by design
explain: W^X says a page is never writable and executable at the same moment. An always-RWX page gives any write bug a place to put code that will run. The recommended pattern is to write, then switch the page to read and execute only.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Control-flow integrity: checking where indirect calls land
question: Why do most Clang CFI schemes require link-time optimization (-flto)?
options: Because LTO makes the binary smaller
Because the set of valid targets for each indirect call depends on every function in the program, which is only visible when the whole program is linked
Because CFI checks run in the linker at run time
Because LTO disables ASLR
explain: Each call site's allowed set includes all address-taken functions of the right type across all object files. Only at link time, with the whole program visible, can the compiler build those sets and emit tight checks.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
question: Android enabled UBSan integer-overflow checks across the media stack. What happens at run time when a crafted file makes `size + chunk_size` overflow?
options: The sum silently wraps and the copy overflows, as before
The check detects the overflow and the process aborts, turning a heap overflow into a crash
The compiler rejects the file
The value is clamped to SIZE_MAX and parsing continues
explain: The sanitizer inserts a check after the addition; on overflow it aborts. Abort is a denial of service at worst, while the unchecked version led to heap corruption and possible code execution.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Core 0 holds line L in Exclusive state and writes to it. What must happen first?
options: Nothing: Exclusive means no other copy exists, so the line silently becomes Modified
An RFO is broadcast to invalidate other copies
The line is written back to main memory
Core 0 must first move the line to Shared
explain: That is the whole point of the Exclusive state: Drepper notes a local write in E does not have to be announced, and that E to M is much faster than S to M. Trouble starts only once another core also wants the line.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: In cross-device federated learning, which expectation is realistic for a single round?
options: Every device in the population contributes once per round
The same few hundred devices are reused every round so they can carry state
A few hundred devices are chosen from the much larger set currently available, and some of them will not report back
Devices are addressed by identifier so the server can retry a specific one
explain: Availability is the constraint. Tens of thousands of devices may be checking in, the server picks a few hundred, clients are not individually addressable and are treated as stateless, and 5 percent or more of a round's participants are expected to drop out. Carrying per-client state across rounds is a cross-silo luxury.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
question: A colleague says FedAvg with E = 5 was fine on their IID benchmark, so the non-IID result must be a bug. What is the right response?
options: They are right: FedAvg is split-independent by construction
With IID clients every local optimum equals the global one, so there is nothing to drift toward; the skew is what creates the bias
The IID result must also be biased, just less visibly
Drift only appears when clients have different sample counts
explain: In our IID split every client has curvature 10/3 and local optimum 2.3, so the fixed point is 2.3 for any E and larger E is pure speedup. Unequal sample counts alone are harmless, since FedAvg already weights by n_k; what hurts is local objectives that disagree with the pooled one.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation and differential privacy
question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: A team has an existing HNSW index over 500M vectors and cannot afford a long rebuild. Which approach fits best?
options: ACORN-gamma with gamma = 1/s_min
ACORN-1 style two-hop lookups over a standard HNSW-like graph
StitchedVamana with one graph per label
Raise M in the existing HNSW and rebuild
explain: ACORN-1 needs no expanded lists at build time; it reconstructs a denser neighborhood during search. Weaviate took this route: its blog says it kept vanilla HNSW indexing so existing data does not need re-indexing. ACORN-gamma and StitchedVamana both require heavier construction, and raising M flattens the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge
question: A team configures 2 shared + 64 routed quarter-size experts and routes to 8 routed experts, keeping the same 2 shared. Compared with DeepSeekMoE 16B (2 + 6 active), what changed?
options: Nothing; shared experts do not count toward compute
Total parameters rose by 2 experts
Activated expert compute rose from 8 to 10 quarter-experts, i.e. from 2 to 2.5 standard FFNs per token
Only the router cost changed
explain: Shared experts always run, so they count fully toward activated compute. DeepSeekMoE lowers the routed top-K by $K_s$ to keep compute fixed: 2 + 6 = 8 quarter-size experts = 2 FFNs. Using 2 + 8 means 10 quarters = 2.5 FFNs, 25% more expert FLOPs.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: MoE on real hardware: expert parallelism, all-to-all and serving
question: A team switches from 64 experts with top-2 to 256 experts with top-8, each a quarter as wide, keeping active parameters fixed. A step routes 2048 tokens. How many rows does each expert's GEMM get on average, and what changes?
options: 16 rows after the switch, because 4 times as many experts share the tokens
256 rows after the switch, because top-8 sends 4 times as many copies of each token
Nothing changes, because FLOPs per token are equal
64 rows in both designs (2048 x 2 / 64 and 2048 x 8 / 256), so intensity stays near 60, but there are 4 times as many GEMMs, each a quarter the size, and each token goes to 4 times as many experts
explain: Tokens per expert = B x K / N, and K and N both grew 4 times. Rows per expert stay at 64, so each GEMM is still memory-bound at the same intensity, but the same work is now split over 4 times as many smaller launches and dispatch destinations. Fine granularity costs efficiency unless kernels group the experts and batches grow.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Secure Boot keys: PK, KEK, db and dbx
question: A laptop has no PK enrolled. What does the UEFI spec say about writing db?
options: It is impossible
It can be written without a signature check, because the platform is in setup mode
It needs Microsoft's signature
Only the TPM can write it
explain: With no PK the platform is in setup mode, and the signature databases can be written without signature validation. That is why a missing PK is a finding in its own right.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Measured boot: PCRs, extend and what each PCR records
question: Secure Boot is switched off in the setup menu, and nothing else changes. Which PCR is designed to reveal this?
options: PCR0
PCR4
PCR7
PCR12
explain: PFP 1.06 requires the SecureBoot variable and the PK, KEK, db and dbx contents to be measured into PCR7, the Secure Boot policy PCR.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: LogoFAIL, a boot logo parsed by the most trusted code
question: Why did Secure Boot not stop LogoFAIL?
options: Secure Boot was disabled on all affected devices
Secure Boot verifies executables before running them; a logo is data parsed by already-trusted firmware code
The logos were signed by Microsoft
Secure Boot only runs after the OS starts
explain: The vulnerable code is the trusted firmware itself. Feeding it malicious data needs no unsigned executable, so nothing for Secure Boot to reject.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: A defender's firmware playbook, and where to practise
question: Which piece of evidence is hardest for malware already running in the OS kernel to forge?
options: A health report from the local EDR agent
A TPM quote over PCRs with the verifier's fresh nonce, checked against a replayed event log
The Windows event log
A screenshot of the setup menu
explain: The kernel can tamper with agents and logs. It cannot produce a TPM signature over PCR values it cannot reset, bound to a nonce it did not choose.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
question: Your FA3-style kernel (head dimension 128, consumers at 240 registers) spills after you enlarge the key block size $B_c$ from 176 to 256. Which part of the 2-stage pipeline is most directly to blame?
options: The extra $S_{next}$ buffer of $B_r \times B_c$ FP32 values kept in registers
The TMA descriptors, which grow with $B_c$
The circular SMEM buffer, which lives in registers
The log-sum-exp vector, which grows with $B_c$
explain: The paper calls out exactly this tradeoff: the 2-stage pipeline holds an extra $S_{next}$ of size $B_r \times B_c \times$ sizeof(float) per thread block, which competes with larger block sizes. SMEM buffers are not in registers, and the log-sum-exp has one value per query row ($B_r$), not per key.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: A decode step for Llama-style GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads. Ignoring other effects, how much does GQA raise attention's operational intensity over plain multi-head attention with the same query count?
options: About 4x, because each KV head serves $g = 4$ query heads
Not at all, decode is always $O(1)$
About 32x, one per query head
It depends only on the page size
explain: The group size is $g = H_{qo}/H_{kv} = 32/8 = 4$. Each key and value loaded from HBM is reused by 4 query heads, so intensity becomes $O(g \cdot l_{qo}) = O(4)$. Page size changes how KV is addressed, not how often each byte is reused.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode in one launch: POD and persistent batches
question: In which batch does fusing prefill and decode attention into one launch help MOST, by the roofline model?
options: 64 decodes of 4K tokens and no prefill
One 8K-token prefill chunk at position 32K and 64 decodes of 1K tokens
A prefill chunk needing about 300 us of math alongside decodes needing about 300 us of KV reads
Any batch, because one launch always halves the time
explain: Overlap saves at most the smaller of the two kernels' bottleneck times, so it pays most when they are similar: about 1.85x in the lesson's model. A decode-only batch has nothing to hide. A huge prefill dwarfs the decodes (5.0 ms of math against 0.08 ms of reads), so the gain is about 2%. One launch can never beat the larger total of compute or memory.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
question: A flow model gives sharp images at 50 Euler steps but blurry, averaged-looking images at 1 step. Which change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Train longer with the same objective
Use a larger batch size
Make the learned paths straighter, for example with reflow or an OT-based coupling
Lower the learning rate at the end of training
explain: A single step follows the initial velocity, which points toward the data mean wherever paths are curved. Training the same objective better converges to the same curved field; straightening the paths is what lets few steps work.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
question: Which bug is TLA+ with TLC best placed to find?
options: An off-by-one in a Rust parsing function
A slow SQL query
A replication protocol that loses committed data if a node crashes during a membership change
A typo in a configuration file
explain: TLA+ checks the design: every interleaving of protocol steps and failures in a small model. Code-level slips like an off-by-one in a Rust function are what Verus-style code proofs (or tests) target.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Modeling a distributed protocol: messages, loss and duplication
question: With WF_vars(Next) and a TMCrash action, Termination fails with r3 stuck in prepared. Which change makes Termination hold while keeping crashes in the model?
options: Let the TM recover with its durable state (tmPrepared survives the crash), or replace the single TM with a replicated coordinator
Add strong fairness on TMCommit
Remove the Consistent invariant
Switch msgs to FIFO sequences
explain: Nothing is enabled for r3 after a permanent crash, so no fairness condition can force progress. Progress needs the decision maker to come back or to be replicated, the idea behind Paxos Commit. TLC confirms the first fix for a TM that may crash once and then recovers: Termination holds over 640 states. FIFO channels change ordering, not the missing decision.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
question: You maintain a Go service that implements a TLA+ spec of a leader-lease protocol. The spec passes TLC, but you suspect the code has drifted from it. What is the cheapest step that would detect drift?
options: Rewrite the service in Rust and verify it with Verus
Prove the spec with TLAPS
Log the service's protocol events in integration tests and check the traces against the spec with TLC
Increase the model size in TLC
explain: Drift is a code-versus-spec question. Trace validation answers it using tests you already run, as the etcd and CCF projects do. TLAPS and bigger models only say more about the spec; a Verus rewrite would work but costs far more.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: GEMMs take 60% of a BF16 training step. FP4 makes them 4x faster and nothing else changes. What is the best possible step speedup?
options: About 1.8x
4x
explain: 1 / ((1 - 0.6) + 0.6 / 4) = 1 / (0.4 + 0.15) = 1.82. The 40% that is not GEMM work now dominates the step. Casting overhead would lower it further.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: You apply stochastic rounding to every tensor, including forward-pass activations and weights. What does the NVFP4 report predict?
options: Better accuracy, since all bias is removed
Worse results: SR on forward tensors adds quantization noise; it pays off mainly on gradients, where bias accumulates
No change, because SR and nearest rounding have the same expected value
Training cannot start, since SR is undefined for weights
explain: SR trades bias for variance. For gradients, which are summed across many steps and microbatches, removing bias matters most. For forward tensors the extra noise simply makes each forward pass less accurate, which the report found harmful.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Credential stuffing at scale, and 23andMe's relatives
question: What made the 23andMe incident so much larger than 14,000 accounts?
options: The attacker cracked the password database
An API returned all users' data without authentication
A sharing feature let each taken account read data about many relatives
The attacker bribed an employee
explain: Per the company, about 14,000 accounts were accessed by credential stuffing, and through DNA Relatives and Family Tree they reached about 6.9 million profiles. Feature design set the blast radius.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
question: Your signup form shows a CAPTCHA, but bot signups did not fall at all. The browser sends `captcha_ok=1` after a successful solve. What is the most likely flaw?
options: The puzzle is too easy
Bots are using residential proxies
The CAPTCHA is not localised
The server trusts a client-set field instead of verifying a token with the challenge service
explain: Scripts never load the puzzle; they post `captcha_ok=1` directly. The server must verify a token server-side, as Stripe's guidance stresses. Easy puzzles or proxies would reduce effectiveness, not eliminate it entirely.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
question: A stolen card number is used on your online shop. The issuer approved it. Two months later the real cardholder disputes it. Without 3-D Secure, who usually bears the loss?
options: The merchant
The issuer, because it approved the payment
The card network
The cardholder
explain: For card-not-present fraud the default rules put the loss on the merchant through the chargeback. Authentication such as 3-D Secure can shift that liability to the issuer (lesson 14).

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
question: A new 3-D Secure flow loses 40% of good customers who face it. What happens to the range of scores where step-up is the best action?
options: It narrows, because each challenge now costs more in lost good orders
It widens
It is unchanged
Step-up becomes best everywhere
explain: The step-up cost term $(1-p)dG$ grows with d, so step-up beats allow only at higher p and beats block only at lower p. Measuring abandonment is part of measuring a control.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme
question: A new rule looks great in a backtest. What is the safest way to launch it?
options: Turn it on for all traffic at once to stop fraud quickly
Launch it only on weekends
Run it in shadow mode to measure would-be hits against maturing labels, then enable it gradually
Announce the rule publicly as a deterrent
